case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Supremacy Clause (and related federal wartime interests reflected in the FTCA’s combatant-activities exception) preempts state tort suits against a military contractor for conduct undertaken while supporting U.S. overseas combat operations.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. VI, cl. 2 (Supremacy Clause), with the Federal Tort Claims Act combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), functioning as the primary federal policy/structure argued to create preemptive force (and with Boyle-style federal common-law displacement as a related doctrine).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Hencely and supporting amici argue that state-law tort claims against contractors are not categorically preempted merely because they arise in a combat zone; the FTCA’s combatant-activities exception is an immunity/retention-of-sovereign-immunity rule for suits against the United States, not a blanket shield for private contractors. They contend preemption (or federal common-law displacement) should be limited—consistent with Boyle—to situations where state tort duties conflict with specific federal directives or military decisions, and where the contractor acted under reasonably precise government specifications or orders. In their view, allowing ordinary negligence or products/warnings-type claims that target the contractor’s own misconduct does not second-guess the military’s combat judgments, does not frustrate the FTCA’s purposes, and preserves compensation/deterrence when contractors, not the government, are the alleged wrongdoers.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Fluor and supporting amici (including the United States) argue that when contractors act within the scope of duties supporting the military’s overseas combat activities, state tort litigation intrudes on uniquely federal interests—wartime command, logistics, force protection, and operational discretion—and risks indirect judicial regulation of combat operations through state-law standards and juries. They maintain the FTCA’s combatant-activities exception embodies a federal policy of eliminating tort-based second-guessing of combat-related conduct and that this policy would be undermined if plaintiffs could simply sue contractors instead of the government. Respondents therefore urge broad Supremacy Clause preemption (often framed as “combatant-activities preemption”) for contractor conduct closely connected to combat operations, at least where the contractor was performing assigned wartime functions under military direction.
key_precedents: Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., 487 U.S. 500 (1988)
Ohio Supreme Court decision declining to adopt Boyle (referenced in the record excerpt: Strickland v. Alert Fire & Safety Equip., Inc., 567 N.E.2d 1027 (Ohio 1991))

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the pragmatic one: even “ordinary” negligence claims can invite intrusive discovery and jury second-guessing of wartime tradeoffs. But under Boyle, that concern must be operationalized through a demonstrated, conduct-specific “significant conflict” with concrete federal direction; otherwise we risk creating a field-like contractor immunity that § 2680(j)’s text (as Justice Kagan notes) does not supply and that our federal-common-law methodology does not authorize. Justice Thomas is right that an FTCA exception can “suggest the outlines” of a federal rule, but that suggestion cannot substitute for Boyle’s limiting principle—some reasonably definite military order/specification (or functional equivalent) plus contractor conformance—lest we immunize independent contractor negligence the Government neither required nor controlled. I therefore stay with petitioner on a narrow preemption rule that protects command prerogatives where genuinely implicated while preserving state-law remedies where they are not.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch are right that § 2680(j) is textually a limitation on the United States’ waiver of sovereign immunity and does not itself confer “immunity” on contractors; I do not rest my position on a contractor-reading of that text. But Boyle’s federal-common-law inquiry asks whether a uniquely federal interest and a significant conflict exist, and combatant activities present a structural conflict because applying state tort duties to conduct integrated into wartime operations inevitably regulates federal command decisions—even when there is no procurement-style “reasonably precise specification” to point to. Roberts’s proposed narrowing risks being underinclusive by treating written directives as the exclusive proxy for conflict outside Boyle’s design-defect setting; operational control and integration into combat functions can be the functional equivalent of a directive where adjudication would necessarily second-guess military judgments. Justice Sotomayor’s compensation and deterrence concerns are policy arguments that cannot overcome the Constitution’s assignment of war powers to the national government and the need for a uniform federal rule in that narrow, combat-integrated context.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the strongest textual point for Petitioner: § 2680(j) is written as a limit on the United States’ FTCA waiver and does not itself confer immunity on contractors, so we should not pretend the statute directly answers the private-defendant question. But that does not defeat Respondent under Boyle, which allows an FTCA exception to “suggest the outlines” of federal common law where uniquely federal interests are implicated; here, as Justice Thomas emphasizes, combatant activities and unified command present a paradigmatic federal interest, and state tort duties applied to contractor conduct under military control create a structural “significant conflict” by forcing jury review and discovery into operational judgments. Roberts’s proposed “reasonably precise specifications” requirement is an ill fit for combat-operations claims that turn on real-time force-protection tradeoffs rather than procurement-style directives, and his approach would invite artful pleading to repackage combat judgment calls as “ordinary negligence.” The limiting principle I would apply is not field-like immunity for any war-zone misconduct, but displacement when the challenged conduct is integrated into combatant activities and performed under military direction such that adjudication would necessarily intrude on wartime decisionmaking—precisely the interference § 2680(j) reflects even if it does not textually name contractors.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the pragmatic one: even “ordinary negligence” suits can drive intrusive discovery and invite juries to second-guess wartime tradeoffs. But Boyle already translates that institutional concern into a legally administrable limit—requiring a demonstrated, conduct-specific “significant conflict” with federal direction (typically reasonably precise orders/specifications plus conformance)—rather than the structural, near-categorical displacement Justice Thomas would infer from mere integration into combat operations. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, § 2680(j) is a sovereign-immunity retention provision for the United States, and using it to create broad contractor preemption untethered to any federal directive stretches federal common law beyond Boyle’s caution and risks immunizing contractor-side negligence the military did not require. My pragmatic methodology favors a rule that protects unified command where the contractor is implementing federal wartime judgments, while preserving compensation and deterrence where harm flows from avoidable, independent contractor misconduct.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest practical point: even “ordinary negligence” suits can intrude on combat decisionmaking through discovery and hindsight jury review. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Boyle requires translating that concern into a conduct-specific “significant conflict” with federal direction; otherwise we are effectively creating field-like preemption from § 2680(j), which by its text is only a limit on the United States’ waiver of immunity. Justice Thomas’s “categorical in kind” theory—preemption whenever conduct is integrated into combatant activities—lacks a workable textual limiting principle and risks immunizing contractor negligence the military did not require or control. A tailored Boyle-style rule (concrete military direction plus conformance) is the pragmatic middle ground that protects federal warfighting interests without untethered expansion of federal common law.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito offer the strongest opposing point: even absent “reasonably precise specifications,” state tort suits over contractor conduct integrated into combat operations can functionally regulate military judgments through discovery and jury hindsight. But under Boyle’s own separation-of-powers logic, that policy concern must be anchored to a demonstrated, conduct-specific “significant conflict” with a federal directive or requirement; otherwise we are announcing a field-like federal common-law immunity based on prudence rather than enacted law. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, § 2680(j) is textually a limitation on the United States’ waiver of sovereign immunity, and converting that carveout into a categorical preemption rule for private parties would expand federal common law beyond any clear congressional instruction. Justice Kavanaugh’s uniformity argument is weighty, yet uniformity alone cannot supply the missing conflict without collapsing Boyle’s limiting principle and immunizing contractor negligence the Government neither ordered nor controlled.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest separation-of-powers point: § 2680(j) is textually about the United States’ retained immunity and cannot, by itself, be transmuted into a free-floating contractor shield. But I agree with Justice Thomas and Justice Alito that Boyle’s “suggest the outlines” framework is not confined to procurement design specifications; it asks whether there is a uniquely federal interest and a significant conflict, and combatant activities conducted under military control present a structural conflict because state tort duties would indirectly regulate operational wartime judgments and force intrusive, command-disruptive litigation. Still, Roberts is right that we must avoid war-zone field preemption, so the rule must be tight: displacement only when the contractor’s challenged conduct is integrated into combat operations and performed under military direction such that adjudication would necessarily second-guess military judgments. That limited approach stays within Boyle’s logic, respects § 2680(j)’s role as a guidepost rather than a grant of immunity, and preserves state remedies for contractor-independent misconduct.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that state tort suits can indirectly regulate combat decisionmaking and impose discovery burdens that intrude on wartime command. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 2680(j) is textually a limitation on the United States’ waiver of sovereign immunity; under Boyle it can “suggest the outlines” of federal common law only when there is a demonstrated, conduct-specific “significant conflict” with concrete federal direction, not a categorical displacement based solely on war-zone integration. Justice Kavanaugh’s “structural conflict” framing is forceful, yet without a requirement analogous to reasonably precise orders/specifications and conformance, it risks converting a jurisdictional carveout into field-like preemption for private defendants—an expansion untethered to enacted text and inconsistent with Boyle’s limiting principle. I therefore remain open to preemption where adjudication would necessarily second-guess specific military judgments the contractor was directed to implement, but I cannot accept respondents’ broader rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the real-world intrusion problem: discovery and jury negligence review can, in practice, pressure military decisionmaking even absent a clear written order. But under Boyle, that practical concern must be operationalized through a conduct-specific “significant conflict” with federal direction; otherwise we are creating categorical field-like immunity from a policy intuition rather than a legally supplied conflicting federal duty, which is the separation-of-powers problem Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize. Justice Thomas’s reliance on § 2680(j) remains insufficient for me because it is a limitation on the United States’ waiver of sovereign immunity, and treating it as a broad anti-tort “policy” that automatically displaces state law for private contractors would expand federal common law beyond Boyle’s limiting principle. A tailored rule—preempting only where the contractor shows reasonably concrete military direction (or functional equivalent) plus conformance such that adjudication would necessarily second-guess that direction—best protects wartime command while preserving remedies for contractor-side negligence not compelled by federal command.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), by its terms preserves sovereign immunity for the United States; it does not itself supply a categorical federal rule immunizing private contractors from state tort law. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., 487 U.S. 500 (1988), displacement/preemption is justified only where there is a “significant conflict” between a uniquely federal interest and state law, and the contractor acted pursuant to reasonably precise governmental specifications (with conformance and adequate warning), which counsels against an across-the-board “combatant-activities preemption” for all contractor conduct in a theater of war. A narrower rule—preempting only claims that would effectively second-guess specific military directives or operational judgments implemented by the contractor—better respects federal wartime interests while adhering to precedent’s limiting principles and avoiding an unnecessary expansion of federal common law. That restrained approach also serves institutional legitimacy by deciding no more than needed and leaving broader contractor immunity to Congress rather than judicial implication from § 2680(j).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause requires state tort law to yield where it significantly conflicts with federal wartime interests, and the FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), reflects an original and textually grounded federal policy of removing tort liability from the conduct of combat operations. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., 487 U.S. 500 (1988), FTCA exceptions can “suggest the outlines” of federal common-law displacement where “uniquely federal interests” are present; combat operations are quintessentially federal and not subject to varying state standards. Allowing state juries to impose negligence duties on contractors performing assigned functions under military direction would indirectly regulate battlefield decisionmaking and logistics in a manner incompatible with § 2680(j)’s structure and purpose. Accordingly, state tort suits are preempted at least for contractor conduct closely connected to combatant activities and carried out under military control.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause requires state tort law to give way where it significantly conflicts with uniquely federal interests, and overseas combat operations present such an interest in unified wartime command and avoiding tort-based second-guessing of battlefield logistics. Although 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j) by its terms preserves the United States’ immunity, it reflects a strong federal policy to keep tort litigation from regulating “combatant activities,” and that policy would be undermined if plaintiffs could evade it by suing contractors performing assigned wartime functions under military direction. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., state law is displaced where there is a “significant conflict” with federal interests, and here imposing state-law duties through juries risks operational interference and uncertainty incompatible with combat operations. Practical consequences reinforce that conclusion: allowing such suits would deter essential contractor support and invite intrusive discovery into military decisionmaking.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not warrant a categorical “combatant-activities preemption” that wipes out ordinary state tort remedies against private contractors merely because the alleged misconduct occurred in a war zone. The FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), is a limitation on the United States’ waiver of sovereign immunity, not an affirmative grant of immunity to contractors, and extending it wholesale would deny compensation and deterrence for contractor negligence without a clear congressional command. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., displacement of state law requires a “significant conflict” with uniquely federal interests and is confined by the “reasonably precise specifications”/government-direction criteria; absent proof that the challenged conduct was specifically directed and tightly controlled by the military, state law should remain available. A narrower, fact-specific Boyle-style inquiry protects legitimate wartime command interests while preserving access to justice for injured individuals, including vulnerable service members and civilians.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), is a retention-of-sovereign-immunity provision for suits against the United States; its text does not by itself create a categorical shield for private contractors from state tort law. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., federal displacement/preemption is appropriate only where there is a “significant conflict” with uniquely federal interests and, critically, where the contractor’s challenged conduct is tied to government-approved, reasonably precise specifications or directions—limits that prevent converting wartime context into a preemption rubber stamp. A broad “combatant-activities preemption” rule risks incoherence and unworkability by immunizing contractor negligence untethered to military judgments, while a Boyle-style, conflict-based approach adequately protects federal wartime command interests when state duties would force second-guessing of actual military decisions. Accordingly, I would reverse and allow the claims to proceed unless the contractor can show the kind of concrete conflict and government control Boyle requires.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not itself confer a freewheeling judicial power to displace state tort law; preemption requires an actual conflict with federal law, and the FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), by its terms addresses the United States’ retention of sovereign immunity rather than granting contractors a categorical tort shield. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., federal common-law displacement is limited to situations presenting a “significant conflict” between a uniquely federal interest and state law, and that conflict is established only where the Government approved reasonably precise specifications (or similarly specific wartime directives), the contractor conformed, and the contractor warned of known dangers. Where the alleged negligence targets the contractor’s own supervisory or operational misconduct that could have complied with both the contract and state duties, Boyle’s conflict requirement is not met and broad “combatant-activities preemption” would improperly expand federal common law at the expense of state authority. Respect for separation of powers counsels leaving any broader contractor immunity to Congress, not courts, particularly when § 2680(j) is silent as to private defendants.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause requires state law to yield where it creates a significant conflict with uniquely federal interests, and wartime combat operations are at the core of those interests. The FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), reflects a federal policy of keeping tort litigation from second-guessing combat-related decisions and disrupting military command and force-protection judgments; allowing state tort suits against contractors performing assigned wartime functions risks reintroducing that battlefield tort regime indirectly. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., displacement is appropriate where state duties would significantly conflict with federal policy, and the contractor’s conduct is closely tied to military direction in combat operations such that state-law standards would regulate federal wartime conduct in practice. As a matter of practical workability and institutional concerns, a broader preemption rule for combat-support activities under military control better preserves uniformity and avoids fifty-state jury oversight of combat logistics and operational decisionmaking.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause preempts state law only where federal law supplies a conflicting rule or where a significant conflict makes state law an obstacle to federal objectives; the FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), by its text addresses when the United States retains sovereign immunity and does not itself create contractor immunity or a broad field-preemptive regime. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., 487 U.S. 500 (1988), any federal common-law displacement must be tightly tied to a “uniquely federal interest” and a “significant conflict” with state tort duties—typically shown by reasonably precise governmental specifications or directives that the contractor followed—rather than categorical preemption for all conduct in a combat zone. Extending Boyle into blanket “combatant-activities preemption” would move beyond the statute’s text and Boyle’s limiting principles and would risk creating federal policy-based immunity without clear congressional authorization, especially where the claims target the contractor’s own alleged negligence rather than military decisions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not justify a broad, categorical “combatant-activities preemption” for private contractors simply because conduct occurred in a combat zone; FTCA § 2680(j) is a retention-of-sovereign-immunity provision for suits against the United States, and it says nothing about immunizing contractors. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., 487 U.S. 500 (1988), displacement/preemption turns on a specifically identified “uniquely federal interest” and a “significant conflict” between state tort duties and federal directives; that limiting framework is not satisfied merely by invoking wartime interests at a high level of generality. Where plaintiffs’ claims can target the contractor’s own negligence or contractual noncompliance without requiring juries to second-guess military command judgments, the practical consequences and procedural fairness concerns counsel against foreclosing state remedies absent clear congressional authorization. Accordingly, I would reject field-like preemption grounded solely in § 2680(j) and require a concrete conflict (e.g., reasonably precise military specifications/orders) before displacing state law.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Supremacy Clause (including federal common-law doctrines tied to wartime/foreign affairs) preempts state tort suits against a military contractor for alleged negligence occurring while the contractor was supporting U.S. overseas combat operations.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Supremacy Clause (U.S. Const. art. VI) and the Federal Tort Claims Act’s “combatant activities” exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), as the asserted source and/or analogue for federal preemptive policy; relatedly, federal common law preemption/immunity doctrines (including Boyle-style displacement).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Hencely argues that state-law tort claims against a government contractor are not categorically displaced merely because the work occurred in a combat zone or supported combat operations. In his view, the FTCA’s combatant-activities exception is a limit on suits against the United States, not a sweeping immunity for private contractors, and it preempts only where a claim would second-guess or directly conflict with military decisions. He further contends the Fourth Circuit’s broad preemption rule departs from this Court’s framework in Boyle by effectively creating a combat-zone contractor immunity untethered to (and broader than) the specific conflict/discretion analysis Boyle requires. Petitioner-side amici (e.g., AAJ, Public Citizen, veterans groups) emphasize accountability, deterrence, and compensation for service members and others injured by contractor negligence that is not mandated or controlled by the military.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Fluor and supporting amici argue that when contractors act within the scope of duties supporting overseas combat activities, state tort law cannot be applied without intruding on uniquely federal interests (war-making, combat operations, foreign affairs) and creating operational conflict with federal wartime policies. They contend the FTCA’s combatant-activities exception reflects a federal policy of eliminating tort liability arising out of combatant activities, and that allowing state suits against contractors would undermine that policy by shifting battlefield-risk costs back onto the federal mission, chilling contractor participation, prompting risk-averse behavior, and inviting judicial scrutiny of combat-zone decisions. Respondents and amici (including the United States, Chamber of Commerce, retired senior military officers, and Atlantic Legal Foundation) therefore favor a broad Supremacy Clause preemption rule for contractor conduct undertaken in support of combat operations, especially where adjudication would require probing military judgments or the conduct of hostilities.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that even allowing these suits can functionally “regulate” warfighting through discovery burdens and jury second-guessing—identifies a serious uniquely federal interest, but under Boyle it cannot by itself satisfy step two’s requirement of a claim-specific “significant conflict” with identifiable federal direction. Section 2680(j), as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, is textually a limit on suits against “the United States,” and treating it as a near-categorical contractor shield risks the very free-floating federal common law expansion O’Melveny warns against, effectively collapsing Boyle into field preemption. Justice Kavanaugh’s limiting principle (preemption when adjudication would probe or contradict hostilities-related military judgments) is the right way to capture the structural war-powers concern without adopting the Fourth Circuit’s overbroad rule; the contractor must make a tailored showing tied to the particular allegations. Because the decision below displaced state law too categorically and without that concrete conflict demonstration, I would reverse and remand under a narrower, administrable test.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s textual point—that § 2680(j) by its terms speaks only to suits against “the United States” and thus cannot be transmuted into categorical contractor immunity—carries weight, and I agree we should not adopt an atextual, geography-based field-preemption rule. But Justice Kavanaugh’s limiting principle essentially concedes the Supremacy Clause conflict I identify: when state tort duties require adjudication that necessarily probes hostilities-integrated military judgments, they function as state regulation of federal war powers, which Boyle permits courts to displace in the face of uniquely federal interests. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s insistence on a claim-specific showing does not negate that, because the conflict arises not just from ultimate liability but from the tort-law standard itself and the litigation machinery (discovery, jury evaluation) intruding into wartime command decisions. Under an originalist and structural Supremacy Clause analysis, I would affirm preemption at least for contractor conduct within the scope of duties supporting combatant activities where adjudication would inherently second-guess such military judgments, even if § 2680(j) is not itself an express contractor-immunity provision.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett are right to stress that § 2680(j) is textually a limit on suits against “the United States,” and O’Melveny cautions against untethered federal common law; that keeps me from endorsing any geography-based, near-field-preemption rule. But Justice Kavanaugh’s focus on whether adjudication would probe hostilities-related military judgments identifies the concrete “significant conflict” Boyle requires in this context: the state-law duty is enforced through a litigation process that will predictably compel discovery and factfinding into operational decisions integrated with combatant activities, functionally reallocating wartime risks Congress and the political branches have placed on the federal side. Justice Sotomayor’s assurance that ordinary negligence doctrines can screen out problematic cases underestimates the practical consequences—litigation burdens and settlement pressure are themselves the regulatory mechanism—so a “claim-specific” test must account for when the elements and proof necessarily intrude on protected military judgments. Properly cabined to integrated combat-support functions and to claims whose adjudication would require second-guessing wartime command decisions, preemption here remains anchored in an identifiable federal conflict rather than free-floating policy.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas press the strongest practical point: litigation—even at the threshold—can intrude on and distort battlefield-integrated decisionmaking through discovery and jury second-guessing. But under Boyle, that operational concern cannot itself supply displacement; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, step two still requires a demonstrated, claim-specific “significant conflict” with identifiable federal direction or a hostilities-related military judgment, and § 2680(j) cannot be transmuted from a limit on suits against the United States into a near-categorical contractor immunity without running into the federal-common-law restraint Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch invoke via O’Melveny. I agree with Justice Kavanaugh that we should craft a workable limiting principle that screens out genuinely intrusive cases early, yet that is an argument for a narrowed conflict test and case management—not for affirming an overbroad rule that forecloses remedies even where contractors deviated from orders or engaged in ordinary negligence not mandated by combat decisions. Because the Fourth Circuit’s approach effectively collapses Boyle’s second step into field preemption, I would reverse and require a concrete, allegation-tethered showing of conflict.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—the litigation-process conflict (intrusive discovery and juries second-guessing battlefield-integrated choices)—is real, but under Boyle it cannot substitute for the step-two requirement of an identifiable, claim-specific “significant conflict” with federal direction or a military judgment actually at issue. As the Chief Justice notes, a near-per-se combat-zone displacement risks collapsing Boyle into field preemption, and § 2680(j)’s text, as Justice Barrett stresses, is a limitation on suits against “the United States,” not a freestanding contractor immunity we may extend via federal common law consistent with O’Melveny’s caution. The workable middle ground is to require an early, concrete proffer showing that the state-law duty would contradict specific military directives or that the claim’s elements necessarily require adjudicating protected hostilities-related judgments, while allowing suits for deviation from orders or non-directed negligence. That approach answers Alito’s administrability concern through threshold management and a tightened conflict test rather than rewriting § 2680(j) into geographic immunity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Supremacy Clause/war-powers framing is the strongest point on the other side, and I accept that state tort duties can, in some circumstances, function as de facto regulation of hostilities; but under Boyle that uniquely federal interest still must cash out in a demonstrated, claim-specific “significant conflict” with identifiable federal duties or decisions. Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize litigation burdens and the risk that discovery and trial will probe battlefield judgments, yet that is an administrability concern that cannot justify converting § 2680(j)—as Justice Barrett stresses, a waiver limit for suits against “the United States”—into a categorical contractor shield, especially given O’Melveny’s warning against free-ranging federal common law. The proper separation-of-powers-limited rule is the Chief Justice’s: reject the Fourth Circuit’s near-per-se combat-zone displacement, but allow preemption when the contractor shows the asserted state-law duty would contradict concrete military directives or necessarily require adjudication of hostilities-integral military judgments. On this record, the Fourth Circuit’s blanket approach is untethered to that required showing, so I remain for reversal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that § 2680(j) is a waiver limitation for suits against the United States and cannot be transmuted into a geography-based, near-field-preemption contractor shield; I agree the Fourth Circuit’s formulation is overbroad. But I remain persuaded that Boyle permits narrowly cabined federal common-law displacement where a claim’s adjudication would necessarily probe and deter hostilities-integrated military judgments, and on these facts the litigation would functionally require second-guessing operational decisions intertwined with combatant activities—creating the “significant conflict” Boyle’s second step demands. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern (via O’Melveny) is serious, but it is met by an opinion that ties preemption to concrete interference with warfighting decisionmaking rather than free-floating policy or generalized combat-zone geography. Justice Sotomayor’s point about preserving suits for deviation or non-directed negligence is important, yet here the asserted state-law duties would still trench on military direction and judgment in a way that practically and institutionally conflicts with uniquely federal war powers.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest contention—that § 2680(j) embodies a federal wartime risk-allocation judgment that contractor tort suits would practically circumvent—identifies a serious federal interest, but it still does not satisfy Boyle’s second-step requirement of a claim-specific “significant conflict” with an identifiable federal directive or protected military judgment. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 2680(j) is textually a limitation on suits against “the United States,” and extending it into near-field preemption for contractors risks the kind of free-floating federal common lawmaking O’Melveny cautions against. Justice Kavanaugh’s concern about intrusive discovery is real, yet under a textualist methodology administrability cannot collapse the conflict inquiry into a categorical combat-support immunity; courts can require an early, concrete proffer showing that the asserted state-law duty would contradict military direction or necessarily adjudicate hostilities-related judgments. I therefore continue to reject the Fourth Circuit’s near-blanket rule while preserving Boyle preemption where a contractor demonstrates a specific, record-grounded conflict on the particular claim.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that even litigating the existence of a conflict can itself intrude on sensitive military judgments through discovery and jury second-guessing—is a serious pragmatic concern, but it is an administrability argument that cannot replace Boyle’s step-two requirement of a claim-specific, identifiable “significant conflict” with federal direction. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s limiting principle better fits both Boyle and the text of § 2680(j), which is a sovereign-immunity/waiver provision for suits against “the United States,” not a categorical contractor shield; extending it into near-field preemption risks the O’Melveny problem Justice Barrett flags (federal common law untethered to enacted law). Justice Thomas’s structural war-powers framing underscores the uniquely federal interest at stake, but under our federal-common-law constraints that interest still must be operationalized through concrete directives or hostilities-integral judgments actually implicated by the pleaded duty, not presumed based on theater or the expected burdens of litigation. The proper way to address Alito/Kavanaugh’s discovery concern is through a tightened conflict test and early, evidence-based proffers (and protective procedures), not by foreclosing claims—including deviation or non-directed negligence—where the military did not meaningfully prescribe the challenged conduct.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not authorize a categorical, combat-zone contractor immunity untethered to Congress’s text, and the FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), is a limitation on suits against the United States—not an automatic preemption of all state tort claims against private parties. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., federal common-law displacement requires both a uniquely federal interest and a showing that the particular state-law claim creates a “significant conflict” with an identifiable federal policy; a per se rule that any contractor liability in a combat setting is preempted skips that second step. A narrower approach—preempting only those claims that would require second-guessing military judgments or that directly conflict with federal wartime directives—better respects federalism and preserves institutional legitimacy while still protecting core warfighting interests. Extending Boyle beyond its procurement/design-defect context to blanket operational negligence immunity would expand federal common law beyond what this Court has permitted absent clear congressional direction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause requires state law to give way where it would operate as a regulation of the Nation’s war powers and the conduct of overseas military operations—subjects the Constitution commits to the Federal Government, not the States. Although 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j) by its terms withdraws FTCA liability only for the United States, it reflects a federal policy to avoid tort-law second-guessing of “combatant activities” and the allocation of battlefield risks, a policy that state tort suits against combat-support contractors would substantially undermine. Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., displacement of state law is appropriate where there is a “uniquely federal interest” and a “significant conflict” between that federal interest and the operation of state law; combat operations and foreign-affairs functions present uniquely federal interests at their apex, and state negligence standards would invite juries to police operational judgments made in theater. Consistent with limited government and federal supremacy in national defense, I would affirm preemption at least for contractor conduct undertaken within the scope of duties supporting combatant activities, rather than allowing state law to impose varying liabilities that interfere with federal wartime objectives.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., state tort law is displaced where it would create a “significant conflict” with uniquely federal interests, and few interests are more uniquely federal than the conduct and support of overseas combat operations. The FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), reflects a federal policy to keep tort litigation from second-guessing wartime operations and to avoid the uncertainty and risk-shifting that civil suits impose on the military mission; allowing state-law negligence suits against contractors performing combat-support functions would substantially undermine that policy as a practical matter. Where adjudication would require probing decisions intertwined with combat support and military judgments, Supremacy Clause-based federal common law must preempt contrary state standards to preserve uniform federal control over wartime conduct. This is consistent with the approach taken by courts relying on § 2680(j) as the analogue for the federal rule of decision in the combat-zone contractor context.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not justify a categorical, combat-zone-wide displacement of state tort law for private contractors, especially where Congress in the FTCA’s “combatant activities” exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), chose to bar suits against the United States—not to confer a sweeping immunity on contractors (see 28 U.S.C. § 2671 excluding contractors). Boyle permits federal common-law displacement only where there is a “significant conflict” between a uniquely federal interest and state law, and it cabined that displacement to circumstances where the Government actually approved or directed the very feature or conduct being challenged; a rule keyed merely to the military’s ultimate command authority is overbroad and untethered to Boyle’s limiting logic. Extending preemption here would unduly foreclose compensation and deterrence for negligent contractor conduct that is not mandated by military judgment, undermining fairness and access to justice for injured service members and other vulnerable plaintiffs. State-law claims should proceed unless respondents can show the claim would second-guess or conflict with specific military decisions, not simply that the conduct occurred in a combat zone.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Boyle v. United Technologies Corp. requires a two-step showing—(1) a uniquely federal interest and (2) a “significant conflict” between that interest and the operation of state tort law—before displacing state law through federal common law, and the Fourth Circuit’s near-categorical combat-zone rule dilutes that conflict inquiry into something closer to field preemption. The FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), is textually a limit on suits against the United States, not an express immunity for contractors, so any Supremacy Clause displacement must be tied to concrete interference with military “battlefield conduct and decision,” not the mere fact of contractor support in a combat theater. A workable middle ground is to allow preemption only where adjudicating the particular negligence claims would require second-guessing military judgments or would impose duties that conflict with military directives—consistent with Boyle’s focus on actual conflict rather than broad policy generalizations. That approach preserves federal wartime interests while avoiding an untethered, contractor-wide immunity that Congress did not enact in § 2680(j).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not itself confer a free-floating power to displace state tort law; any contractor immunity must be anchored in enacted federal law or in the narrow federal-common-law displacement this Court recognized in Boyle, which requires a “significant conflict” between state duties and specific federal interests or obligations. 487 U.S. at 508–09. The FTCA’s “combatant activities” exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), by its plain terms limits the United States’ waiver of sovereign immunity and does not create categorical immunity for private contractors, so it cannot be transformed into broad preemption absent a concrete conflict with federal directives. Applying a blanket combat-zone preemption rule would extend Boyle beyond its limits and risk judicial lawmaking in an area where separation-of-powers principles counsel restraint; at most, preemption should turn on whether state tort duties would require second-guessing or contradicting military judgments in a particular case.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: This case implicates uniquely federal interests in war-making and foreign affairs, where state tort law can create a “significant conflict” with federal policy and operational decisionmaking, triggering displacement under Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., 487 U.S. 500 (1988). The FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), reflects a federal policy to keep tort litigation from regulating or second-guessing combatant activities during time of war, and that policy would be undermined if identical claims could proceed against contractors performing integrated combat-support functions. Consistent with precedent and practical workability, a Supremacy Clause-based federal common-law rule should preempt state claims at least where adjudication would require probing military judgments or the conduct of hostilities, rather than creating a broad, free-floating negligence regime in the combat theater. Given those conflicts and the Court’s institutional interest in avoiding judicial intrusion into battlefield decisions, I would vote to affirm preemption here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not itself create a freewheeling contractor immunity; preemption must be tied to identifiable federal law, and Boyle v. United Technologies Corp. requires (1) a uniquely federal interest and (2) a significant conflict between that interest and the operation of state tort law, with any displacement cabined to what the conflict necessitates. Although overseas combat operations implicate uniquely federal interests, the FTCA’s “combatant activities” exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), is textually a limit on suits against the United States, not a categorical bar to state-law claims against private parties, and it does not supply a broad federal rule automatically displacing all contractor negligence claims in a combat zone. Under Boyle’s conflict-based approach (and this Court’s admonitions in cases like O’Melveny & Myers that federal common law is limited and scope turns on conflict), state tort claims should be preempted only where adjudication would second-guess or directly conflict with military directives or the conduct of hostilities, not merely because the contractor was supporting combat operations. The Fourth Circuit’s broader rule effectively extends § 2680(j) beyond its text and beyond Boyle’s methodology by creating a categorical combat-zone contractor immunity untethered to government direction or a demonstrated, case-specific conflict.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Boyle requires a demonstrated “significant conflict” between a uniquely federal interest and the operation of state tort law, and it cabins any displacement to situations where the Government meaningfully approved or directed the challenged feature or conduct such that state law would effectively second-guess the military’s own decisions. 487 U.S. at 507–12. The FTCA’s combatant-activities exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(j), is a limitation on suits against the United States and, at most, an analogue that may inform the conflict inquiry; it does not itself create a categorical, combat-zone immunity for private contractors. A broad Supremacy Clause rule preempting all negligence claims merely because the conduct occurred in a combat environment risks eliminating accountability for contractor deviation from military orders and contractual duties, without the tailored conflict showing Boyle and this Court’s federal common-law restraint demand. Procedural fairness and practical consequences favor preserving state-law remedies unless adjudication would necessarily intrude on or conflict with specific military judgments about the conduct of hostilities.
